shapes.name: AdminSessionEntry
shapes.description:
A session in the system-wide history, which is a session plus whose it is.

Separate from SessionEntry rather than an extension of it because the two
answer different questions. A person reading their own list wants to know
which row is the browser they are sitting at; an admin reading every row
ever wants to know whose it is, and `current` would be false on all of them.

Every read here is `SELECT USER_COLUMNS`, which is the users table minus the
three columns that must never be published: the password hash, and the reset
token with its expiry.

shapes.name: AdminUserDetail
shapes.description:
Everything about one account that is spread across five tables.

What it deliberately does not carry is as much the point as what it does:
no password hash, no TOTP secret, no recovery codes, and no device tokens or
their hashes. That two-factor is on is administration; the secret behind it
is not, and an endpoint that hands it over turns every admin session into a
way of taking somebody's account.

fields.name: sessions
fields.description: Newest first, capped - see sessionsFor().

fields.name: login_attempts
fields.description: Newest first, the last fifty.

fields.name: recovery_codes_remaining
fields.description: Zero when two-factor is off, rather than a count of nothing.

shapes.name: AdminUserIdentity
shapes.description:
One provider account attached to a site account.

The provider's own permanent id for the person - `subject` - is deliberately
not here. It identifies them to Google and is what the sign-in path matches
on; an admin looking at who is connected has no use for it.

fields.name: provider
fields.description: 'google' today.

fields.name: email
fields.description: The address the provider gave, which is what there is to recognise.

shapes.name: AuthMailRequested
shapes.description:
The answer from the two endpoints that take an address and may send to it.

Always the same, and says nothing about what was found. Whether there is an
account behind an address, whether it still needs confirming, whether it has
a password to reset - none of that is anything an endpoint open to the whole
internet should be willing to tell apart.

shapes.name: AuthPending
shapes.description:
What registration hands back: no session, because there is not one yet.

The account exists and cannot be used until the address on it is confirmed,
so the only useful things to say are which address the message went to and
whether it actually went. `sent` false is not an error - the account is made
either way - but it lets the page offer to try again instead of telling
somebody to go and look for a message that was never posted.

shapes.name: AuthProviders
shapes.description:
Which ways in this deployment offers, asked before anybody has signed in.

The client id is public by design - it travels in the page and identifies
the site to Google - so there is nothing here that the rendered button would
not give away anyway. Null, and `google_enabled` false, while no client id
is configured, which is how the site ships.

fields.name: device_token
fields.description:
A secret for the browser to keep, when it asked to be remembered.

Present only where there was something to remember: an account with
two-factor on, signing in with `remember_device`. Sent back on later
sign-ins to skip the six digits - and nothing else, since the
password still has to be right. Null every other time.

shapes.name: CharacterFull
shapes.description:
`GET /api/characters/{id}/full`

The odd one out: characters predate registerFullResource(), so their costs
come back flat rather than nested under the phase or level they belong to.
The write side nests ascension costs and spells the talent costs
`talent_costs`, which is why the form rebuilds the body rather than putting
back what it was given.

shapes.name: SessionEntry
shapes.description:
One session: where the account was signed in, how, and whether it still is.

`ip` and `user_agent` are what the request carried, unexamined. They are
shown so a person can recognise their own devices, not relied on for
anything - a user agent is a string the caller chooses.

fields.name: method
fields.description: password, login_code, google, or email_link.

fields.name: mac
fields.description:
The caller's hardware address, and null nearly always.

Only knowable when the caller shares a network with the server, and
so is still in its neighbour table - a MAC address does not survive
a router. See requestMac().

fields.name: revoked_reason
fields.description: Why it ended, where anything but its own expiry ended it.

fields.name: active
fields.description: Neither revoked nor expired - worked out here, against our own clock.

fields.name: current
fields.description: The session asking. The page will not offer to end this one by surprise.

shapes.name: SessionList
shapes.description:
Every session this account has had, and how many attempts have failed since
it last succeeded.

The count is deliberately "since the last good sign-in" rather than a
lifetime total: a number that only grows says nothing, and the question
worth answering is whether somebody has been trying lately.

shapes.name: SessionsEnded
shapes.description: How many sessions "sign out everywhere else" actually ended.

shapes.name: ThemeChanged

shapes.name: TotpRecoveryCodes
shapes.description:
The way back in when the phone is gone.

Returned exactly once, when they are generated, because only their hashes
are kept. There is no endpoint that can show them again - asking for another
set replaces them.

shapes.name: TotpSetup
shapes.description:
A freshly issued two-factor secret, on its way to an authenticator app.

Both forms of the same thing: the URI is what a QR code encodes, and the
secret is what somebody types when there is no camera to hand. Nothing is
required of the account until a code computed from it has been handed back.

fields.name: secret
fields.description: Base32, as an authenticator expects it typed.

fields.name: uri
fields.description: The otpauth:// URI a QR code carries.
